blocks.orig: Every year, over 30,000 people attempt to climb Kilimanjaro, and for many, it is a once-in-a-lifetime experience.
blocks.html: More than 30,000 people try to climb Kilimanjaro each year, and for many of them it is an experience that happens only once in a lifetime.

blocks.orig: In order to help those who are interested in Kilimanjaro trekking learn what they need to know, we’ve put together this beginner’s guide to climbing Mount Kilimanjaro.
blocks.html: To give anyone thinking about Kilimanjaro trekking the information they need, we’ve written this beginner’s guide to climbing Mount Kilimanjaro.

blocks.orig: Climbing Kilimanjaro is not as easy as you might think. As such, it’s crucial that you be totally prepared for your mountain trek, including knowing how and when is the best time to climb it.
blocks.html: Kilimanjaro is harder to climb than you may expect. That is why being fully prepared for your trek is essential, and that includes knowing how to climb it and when the best time is.

blocks.orig: In addition to that, you need to make sure you have the right gear as well. Your equipment and knowledge about your destination will ensure you stay safe during your climb.
blocks.html: You also need to be sure that you bring the right equipment. Good gear and knowing your destination will keep you safe on the way up.

blocks.orig: We have created the ultimate beginner’s guide to trekking Kilimanjaro. Follow our advice and get ready to take on the mountain.
blocks.html: Here is our complete beginner’s guide to trekking Kilimanjaro. Take our advice on board and get ready to tackle the mountain.

blocks.orig: Kilimanjaro is situated in the northeastern region of the nation, close to the Kenya-Tanzania border. Arusha and Kilimanjaro International Airport are the closest cities and airports (airport code JRO).
blocks.html: You will find Kilimanjaro in the northeast of the country, near the border between Kenya and Tanzania. The nearest city is Arusha and the nearest airport is Kilimanjaro International Airport (airport code JRO).

blocks.orig: Three volcanic cones — Kibo, Mawenzi, and Shira — create Tanzania’s dormant volcano, which we know as Kilimanjaro volcano.
blocks.html: Tanzania’s dormant volcano, known to us as Kilimanjaro volcano, is made up of three volcanic cones — Kibo, Mawenzi and Shira.

blocks.orig: Kilimanjaro is 5,895 meters (19,340 ft) above sea level. In addition to being the highest freestanding mountain in the world, it is also the highest point in Africa.
blocks.html: Kilimanjaro rises 5,895 meters (19,340 ft) above sea level. It is the highest point in Africa as well as the tallest freestanding mountain in the world.

blocks.orig: When Is The Best Time Of The Year To Climb Mount Kilimanjaro?
blocks.html: When in the year should you climb Mount Kilimanjaro?

blocks.orig: One of the two dry seasons is the ideal time to climb Kilimanjaro. Given its position in Tanzania, the region only experiences two seasons: the wet and the dry.
blocks.html: The best moment to climb Kilimanjaro is during one of the two dry seasons. Because of where it lies in Tanzania, the area has just two seasons: wet and dry.

blocks.orig: It is dry most of the time from July through October. Between December and February is the second dry season. These two windows are excellent for trekking Mount Kilimanjaro.
blocks.html: From July to October it is mostly dry. The second dry season falls between December and February. Both periods are excellent for trekking Mount Kilimanjaro.

blocks.orig: If you’re an experienced traveler, you could try Kilimanjaro trekking during the wet season, but we would highly suggest you avoid doing this. You are more likely to fail, so it is best to wait for the dryer seasons, which are also safer.
blocks.html: Experienced travellers could attempt Kilimanjaro trekking in the wet season, though we strongly advise against it. Your chances of failing are higher, so it is better to wait for the drier seasons, which are safer too.

blocks.orig: How Long Does It Take To Climb Up Kilimanjaro?
blocks.html: How many days does a Kilimanjaro climb take?

blocks.orig: Depending on the path chosen, trekking Mount Kilimanjaro can take as little as 5 days or as long as 9 days.
blocks.html: Trekking Mount Kilimanjaro takes anywhere from 5 to 9 days, depending on the route you choose.

blocks.orig: There are 8 recognized Kilimanjaro routes: Umbwe, The Western Breach, Machame, Lemosho, Shira, Rongai, Northern Circuit, and Shira. Which all come from various locations on the mountain.
blocks.html: Kilimanjaro has 8 recognised routes: Umbwe, The Western Breach, Machame, Lemosho, Shira, Rongai, Northern Circuit and Shira. Each of them starts from a different point on the mountain.

blocks.orig: It is common knowledge that half of those who try climbing will fail. You can avoid it by taking longer routes – these are also known to significantly raise the Kilimanjaro trekking success rate.
blocks.html: It is widely known that half of all climbers do not succeed. You can prevent this by choosing a longer route – longer routes are known to raise the Kilimanjaro trekking success rate considerably.

blocks.orig: The most successful approaches have success rates of 85% to 95% and span between 8 and 9 days.
blocks.html: The routes with the best results take 8 to 9 days and have success rates of 85% to 95%.

blocks.orig: Some tour guides advise travelers to book the five-day Marangu Route, often known as the “Tourist” route, because it is the cheapest and “easiest” option.
blocks.html: Some tour guides recommend the five-day Marangu Route, often called the “Tourist” route, as it is the cheapest and “easiest” choice.

blocks.orig: Unfortunately, the success rate for this approach is low, all because of height acclimatization.
blocks.html: Sadly, this route has a low success rate, entirely due to altitude acclimatization.

blocks.orig: This is because people don’t have enough time to get used to the little air the higher up the mountain you get. However, it is a popular route because on your way, you’ll come across huts to sleep in.
blocks.html: The reason is that climbers do not get enough time to adjust to the thin air as they go higher up the mountain. It remains popular, however, because there are huts to sleep in along the way.

blocks.orig: Still, the top section is extremely steep, which makes completing the climb difficult.
blocks.html: Even so, the final section is very steep, which makes finishing the climb hard.

blocks.orig: Why Is Trekking Kilimanjaro Seen As Difficult?
blocks.html: Why do people consider Kilimanjaro trekking hard?

blocks.orig: Trekking Kilimanjaro is very much possible, although it is considered a difficult feat. On the trails, there seems to be little exposure or chance of injury from a fall. Furthermore, there are no technical climbs, as well as no steep drops.
blocks.html: You can certainly trek Kilimanjaro, even though it is regarded as a tough challenge. The trails offer little exposure and little risk of injury from falling. There are also no technical climbs and no steep drops.

blocks.orig: Although there are a few brief spots that call for some scrambling (hands and feet), the rest of the ascent just entails hiking.
blocks.html: Apart from a few short stretches where you need to scramble (using hands and feet), the climb is simply hiking.

blocks.orig: However, it’s the elevation that makes it challenging. The amount of oxygen in the air at the top of Kilimanjaro is around half what it is at sea level.
blocks.html: What makes it hard is the altitude. At the summit of Kilimanjaro, the air contains roughly half the oxygen found at sea level.

blocks.orig: The body experiences stress when operating in low oxygen conditions. To keep operating at high altitudes without becoming ill, the body must adjust. The key to reducing the likelihood of altitude sickness is gradual ascent.
blocks.html: Working with little oxygen puts the body under stress. It has to adapt so it can keep going at high altitude without falling ill. Climbing gradually is the key to lowering the risk of altitude sickness.

blocks.orig: Is A Guide Required To Climb Mount Kilimanjaro?
blocks.html: Do you need a guide to climb Mount Kilimanjaro?

blocks.orig: Anyone climbing Mount Kilimanjaro must have a licensed guide from Kilimanjaro National Park with them at all times.
blocks.html: Every climber on Mount Kilimanjaro must be accompanied at all times by a licensed guide from Kilimanjaro National Park.

blocks.orig: Most climbers have a crew that includes a lead guide, an assistant guide, a cook, and porters. However, it is essential to always have a guide and follow what they say.
blocks.html: Most climbers have a team made up of a lead guide, an assistant guide, a cook and porters. Whatever the set-up, you must always have a guide with you and do as they say.

blocks.orig: They have done that route hundreds of times, so they will know what is best to keep you and anyone else safe.
blocks.html: Having walked the route hundreds of times, they know best how to keep you and everyone else safe.

blocks.orig: Temperatures And Campsites On Mount Kilimanjaro
blocks.html: Temperatures and campsites on Mount Kilimanjaro

blocks.orig: Some people believe that Kilimanjaro never gets cold because it is located in Africa, which is associated with extremely hot temperatures.
blocks.html: Some people think Kilimanjaro is never cold, since it lies in Africa, a continent linked with very hot weather.

blocks.orig: On the other hand, the mountain’s summit is extremely chilly and blustery, especially at night. Here, the coldest temperatures are typically between 20 and -20 degrees Celsius.
blocks.html: In fact, the summit of the mountain is very cold and windy, particularly at night. The lowest temperatures here usually range between 20 and -20 degrees Celsius.

blocks.orig: As a result, if you’re serious about your Kilimanjaro trekking adventure, you must pack the correct clothing to help you against these chilly temperatures. Thermals are a must, as are some solid walking boots.
blocks.html: So if you take your Kilimanjaro trekking adventure seriously, you need to bring the right clothing to protect you from the cold. Thermals are essential, and so is a pair of sturdy walking boots.

blocks.orig: When climbing Kilimanjaro, you camp for the most part. There is one route which does have sleeping huts. Although it is more common for you to camp.
blocks.html: On a Kilimanjaro climb you mostly sleep in a tent. One route has huts to sleep in, but camping is much more usual.

blocks.orig: Even though you may be camping, there are no campfires permitted on the mountain. Open fires just cannot be supported by the available wood. Meals are prepared on burners powered by propane.
blocks.html: Although you will often be camping, campfires are not allowed on the mountain. There is simply not enough wood to sustain open fires. Food is cooked on propane burners.

blocks.orig: Each campsite has public restrooms, which are cleaned regularly. However, when the camp is busy, the restrooms can become a bit dirty. Some companies that you book with may provide you with a portable restroom to use.
blocks.html: At every campsite there are public toilets that are cleaned regularly. When a camp is crowded, though, they can get rather dirty. Some companies may supply you with a portable toilet.

blocks.orig: Finally, you won’t experience any kind of amenities (like washrooms or showers) when trekking Kilimanjaro. You can bring baby wipes and use them to clean yourself off if you want to. However, most people deal with not showering for a maximum of 9 days.
blocks.html: Lastly, there are no facilities at all (such as washrooms or showers) while trekking Kilimanjaro. If you like, you can pack baby wipes to freshen up. Most people simply cope with going without a shower for up to 9 days.

blocks.orig: There is certainly a lot of equipment needed to climb Kilimanjaro. Beginning in the rainforest and reaching its peak in the Arctic zone, the ascent passes through several unique ecological zones.
blocks.html: You definitely need quite a lot of gear to climb Kilimanjaro. The climb starts in the rainforest and ends in the Arctic zone at the summit, crossing several distinct ecological zones along the way.

blocks.orig: Your mountaineering attire should be capable of keeping you warm, dry, and protected from the elements during cold and wet weather.
blocks.html: Your mountain clothing must keep you warm and dry and shield you from the elements when it is cold and wet.

blocks.orig: You will require equipment, decent footwear, and technical apparel made of waterproof, insulated, and breathable materials. This includes a duffel bag, sleeping bag and day pack.
blocks.html: You will need gear, good footwear and technical clothing made from waterproof, insulated and breathable fabrics. That also means a duffel bag, a sleeping bag and a day pack.

blocks.html: Visitors to Tanzania are advised to be vaccinated against typhoid, hepatitis A and tetanus.

blocks.html: Malaria risk is high in most of Tanzania, so anti-malaria medication is recommended and you must take measures to avoid mosquito bites.

blocks.orig: Wear long sleeves and long pants, especially after sunset, apply insect repellent to exposed skin, and sleep with a mosquito net to prevent mosquito bites.
blocks.html: To avoid mosquito bites, wear long sleeves and long trousers, particularly after dark, put insect repellent on any bare skin and sleep under a mosquito net.

blocks.orig: Due to Kilimanjaro’s elevation above sea level, there are essentially no mosquitoes on the mountain. Nevertheless, Kilimanjaro is considered to be in the rainforest region.
blocks.html: Because Kilimanjaro is so high above sea level, there are practically no mosquitoes on the mountain. Kilimanjaro is nonetheless regarded as part of the rainforest region.
